### Road safety factors

Tables with data to 2023 for contributory factors can be found in the section on tables no longer updated at the bottom of this page.

## Age differences
Based on an analysis of data from 2022 from FARS and the National Household Travel Survey, the number of driver fatal crash involvements per 100 million miles driven in 2022 was 48% higher for males (2.8 per 100 million miles traveled) than for females (1.9 per 100 million miles traveled). Among drivers ages 16-29, rates were substantially higher for males than for females, but the differences were smaller for ages 30-69. Rates were higher for females than for males among drivers ages 70 and over.

## Latest data and table index
The tables below are the latest final annual statistics for 2025, which are currently the latest available final data. Some tables which rely on data from the National Travel Survey diary will be updated alongside the 2026 statistics in summer 2027. Further details of the reasons are available in the additional analysis publication.
Provisional statistics for the first half of 2026 are scheduled for publication in November 2026.
A list of all reported road collisions and casualties data tables and variables in our data download tool is available in the Tables index (ODS, 144 KB).

## Factors contributing to collisions and casualties (RAS07)
### Road safety factors
Following the most recent STATS19 review (PDF, 296KB)contributory factors (CFs) are being replaced by new road safety factors (RSFs),in some police forces from late 2023 onwards. This has resulted in a break in the time series for some of the data. As a result, we are presenting all data using the RSF specification, but separating out data initially recorded as CFs. We do not recommend directly combining this data. As a result, RAS0705 and RAS0706 have been temporarily withdrawn. Further details can be found in our road safety factors guidance.
Tables with data to 2023 for contributory factors can be found in the section on tables no longer updated at the bottom of this page.
From September 2026, we are publishing a further breakdown of CF and RSF data which separates cases where factors are assigned to drivers or riders or pedestrians. These tables present high-level breakdowns and time series.A list of all tables, including those discontinued, is available in the table index. More detailed data is available in our data tools, or by downloading the open dataset.
We have made some minor changes to some of the published tables alongside the publication of the 2025 figures. Further details of these, and planned future changes, can be found alongside the latest statistics and any feedback can be provided via our user feedback survey.

## Latest data and table index
The tables below are the latest final annual statistics for 2025, which are currently the latest available final data. Some tables which rely on data from the National Travel Survey diary will be updated alongside the 2026 statistics in summer 2027. Further details of the reasons are available in the additional analysis publication.
Provisional statistics for the first half of 2026 are scheduled for publication in November 2026.
A list of all reported road collisions and casualties data tables and variables in our data download tool is available in the Tables index (ODS, 144 KB).

## All collision, casualty and vehicle tables
Reported road collisions and casualties data tables (zip file) (ZIP, 5.83 MB)

## Historic trends (RAS01)
RAS0101: Collisions, casualties and vehicles involved by road user type since 1926 (ODS, 36.2 KB)
RAS0102: Casualties and casualty rates, by road user type and age group, since 1979 (ODS, 110 KB)

## Road user type (RAS02)
RAS0201: Numbers and rates (ODS, 25.6 KB)
RAS0202: Sex and age group (ODS, 144 KB)
RAS0203: Rates by mode, including air, water and rail modes (ODS, 24.5 KB)
RAS0204: Enhanced severity and injury type (ODS, 93.1 KB)

## Road type (RAS03)
RAS0301: Speed limit, built-up and non-built-up roads (ODS, 18.5 KB)
RAS0302: Urban and rural roads (ODS, 32.3 KB)
RAS0303: Strategic road network (ODS, 15.3 KB)

## Geographical breakdowns (RAS04)

RAS0403: Local authority (ODS, 1.49 MB)

RAS0405: Combined authority (ODS, 346 KB)

## Vehicles and drivers (RAS05)
RAS0501: Drivers involved by sex, age and road user type (ODS, 94 KB)
RAS0502: Vehicles involved and involvement rates (ODS, 23.2 KB)
RAS0503: Vehicle type and manoeuvre (ODS, 19 KB)
RAS0504: Vehicle type and road type (built up and non built up roads) (ODS, 52.5 KB)
RAS0505: Left-hand drive vehicles (ODS, 30.8 KB)
RAS0506: Journey purpose (ODS, 70.2 KB)
RAS0507: Propulsion type (ODS, 83.7 KB)

## Casualties and vehicles combination (RAS06)
RAS0601: Casualties by vehicle and road user type involved in collision (ODS, 52.8 KB)
RAS0602: Hit and run collisions (ODS, 22.4 KB)

## Factors contributing to collisions and casualties (RAS07)
### Drink-drive collisions
Detailed data tables for drink-drive collisions are shown in section RAS20 below.

## Factors contributing to collisions and casualties (RAS07)
### Road safety factors
Following the most recent STATS19 review (PDF, 296KB)contributory factors (CFs) are being replaced by new road safety factors (RSFs),in some police forces from late 2023 onwards. This has resulted in a break in the time series for some of the data. As a result, we are presenting all data using the RSF specification, but separating out data initially recorded as CFs. We do not recommend directly combining this data. As a result, RAS0705 and RAS0706 have been temporarily withdrawn. Further details can be found in our road safety factors guidance.
Tables with data to 2023 for contributory factors can be found in the section on tables no longer updated at the bottom of this page.
From September 2026, we are publishing a further breakdown of CF and RSF data which separates cases where factors are assigned to drivers or riders or pedestrians. This is presented in table ‘RAS0701 split’ below. We intend to further develop this approach in future road casualty statistics publications and any feedback on the presentation is welcome.
RAS0701: Collisions, casualties and road user type (ODS, 553 KB)
RAS0701 split: Collisions, casualties and road user type (by factor assignment) (ODS, 1.22 MB)
RAS0702: Vehicle type (ODS, 569 KB)
RAS0703: Road class (motorway, A road, B road, other road) (ODS, 109 KB)

### Seatbelt non-wearing

### Drivers and riders involved
RAS2021: By sex of driver or rider (ODS, 19.4 KB)
RAS2022: By age of driver (cars only) (ODS, 14.9 KB)

## Drink-drive collisions and casualties (RAS20)
### Casualties in drink-drive collisions
RAS2031: All casualties by casualty type, sex and age (ODS, 22.5 KB)
RAS2032: Driver and rider fatalities percentage over the legal blood alcohol limit (ODS, 15.4 KB)
RAS2033 : Fatalities aged 16 and over by blood alcohol level (ODS, 15.8 KB)

## Drink-drive collisions and casualties (RAS20)
### Breath tests
Figures on roadside breath tests for England and Wales, previously shown in table RAS51016, are published by the Home Office in their Police Powers and Procedures statistics.
RAS2041: Breath tests drivers or riders involved in reported road collisions in Great Britain (ODS, 14.5 KB)
RAS2042: Screening test results in England and Wales, by reason for test (ODS, 16.6 KB)

## Drink-drive collisions and casualties (RAS20)
### Self-reported drink-driving
Data tables on self-reported drink driving, drug driving and driver mobile phone use are published in our factsheet on self-reported driver behaviour available from the factsheets page.

## Other road safety data (RAS40)
### Cost of preventing collisions
RAS4001: Average and total value of prevention of collisions (ODS, 52.9 KB)

## Other road safety data (RAS40)
### Comparing police road casualty data with other sources
RAS4101: Hospital admissions data on road casualties (ODS, 27.4 KB) - data currently available up to 2020
RAS4201: National Travel Survey self-reported injuries in road collisions (ODS, 36.4 KB)
RAS4301: Death registrations data - this table will be added in due course

## Other road safety data (RAS40)
### Motoring offences
Statistics on motoring offences are published annually by the Ministry of Justice as part of their criminal justice statistics and the Home Office in their police powers and procedures statistics.

## Tables no longer updated

The comma-separated values (CSV) file format is widely used in government for sharing and receiving data. This guidance is for government employees who publish data. It shares the standard and best practice for creating consistent and interoperable CSV files.
The government recommends the RFC 4180 open standard for CSV files. You can read how to use this standard in the Tabular data standard profile.
RFC 4180 aims to reduce common problems and help with data management. The standard and this guidance focus on the manual process and do not refer to using automated tools, libraries and languages. You can use some of the principles in this document in automated environments.

## Using CSV files to meet user needs
When creating a CSV file you should consider the needs of government users such as statisticians, data collection agencies, developers and data engineers.
These users need a consistent CSV file format so they can:
*   make data sets easier to share  
*   aggregate data and publish it as part of the UK’s policy on open data, consistent with the principles of the open data charter  
*   share data in the open for citizens and government workers  
*   make it easier to compare data from different data sets
You should also consider whether your CSV will be read by machines or by humans, and understand how this affects the accessibility needs of your file.
The main benefits of using CSV include the ability to:
*   improve data sharing between government organisations  
*   import and export CSV files to most data and analytic solutions  
*   provide forward and backwards compatibility and adaptability to changing applications and requirements  
*   open smaller files in a simple text editor as CSV uses a plain text format  
*   improve data security - any program or malicious code in the CSV will not run when you open the file in a text editor

## When not to use CSV files
It may not be appropriate to use the CSV file format if you:
*   have large files that you query several times a day - it may be more suitable to use a different format that offers compression capabilities  
*   need greater flexibility to encode additional information in the file beyond the raw data  
*   need to use JSON with REST APIs - you could, however, provide a ‘Download as CSV’ option for non-technical users
It is important to note that exporting a spreadsheet to CSV format will:
*   remove any formatting such as font styles, links, borders and formulas  
*   only export the current tab - single CSV does not support multiple spreadsheet tabs without reorganising your data

## Setting up your CSV file
Before you produce a CSV file, make sure the data is about one subject area. Your columns should relate to each other and not mix unrelated information. For example, you should not put employee records and budget figures in the same CSV file.
When manually setting up a CSV file, or setting up an automated process, you should:
*   include a header row to provide basic information about the file so users or machines do not need to make assumptions about column names  
*   use only one header row - if you have multiple header rows, combine or merge them into a single header row  
*   use one data type per column, for example do not mix numeric data and text in the same column unless you have a valid reason such as marking a value as ‘null’  
*   make your column headers as simple as possible and avoid special characters, for example, ‘time period (mins)’ could become ‘time_period_mins’ or ‘time_period’  
*   use commas to separate fields, especially when publishing data - do not use pipes (also known as the vertical bar symbol ‘`|`’)  
*   avoid using line feed (‘\n’) and carriage return (‘\r’) characters as they can cause data import issues  
*   save the file in UTF-8 - this is an international standard that supports characters in most scripts and minimises errors in the import and export of files  
*   use only one value per cell - do not list multiple values (arrays) in a single cell, for example “value1, value2, value3”
You should also apply metadata to your CSV files. You can learn more by reading the:
*   open standard for CSV on the Web (CSVW)  
*   guidance on recording information about data sets you share with others  
*   open standard for using metadata to describe CSV data  
*   W3C guidance about how to build a metadata file

## Managing large CSV files
The definition of a large CSV file will depend on the department and tool using the file. As a general guide, a CSV file size of a few hundred MB is large for Excel while a CSV file size of a few GB is large for an API or a data management tool. Keep this in mind when choosing which tools or applications to use.
When using large CSV files in Excel, you must make sure the whole file loads properly. If you are using older versions of Excel (97-2003) you should be aware that they have a low row limit of around 65,000 rows. Microsoft has information about Excel specifications and limits.
When CSV files become large, data suppliers might compress them into a ZIP file. If you use a ZIP file, you should add metadata to describe your CSV and add instructions on how to open the ZIP file without causing errors to the contents of the file.

## Validating your CSV files
To make sure your CSV files remain accurate and consistent, you should:
*   check the data does not change when opening the file in common applications - for example, some spreadsheet tools remove leading zeros for values such as ‘0008’  
*   check the application opening your CSV files recognises the column formats and their content, such as time and date  
*   check the characters in the CSV columns to make sure they display correctly  
*   provide guidance on any application specific problems you’re aware of  
*   make sure your CSV files still open correctly if you export them from an application  
*   make sure your chosen tool displays all the rows and columns

## Moving or storing data in CSV file format
When creating data sets, you should consider whether it is likely your data set will need to be transferred to or stored in different places. Using a standardised data structure makes moving data easier and helps keep it intact.

You should not compress multiple database tables into one CSV file. Instead, you could use a format such as CSV on the Web to express the relationships between several separate CSV files, or use a more appropriate file format.
